input: Staffing levels in the quality laboratory have been the subject of considerable discussion in recent months, and this review brings together the key figures that underpin the current debate. The laboratory currently employs 18 full-time staff, and over the course of last year overtime working amounted to 10% of paid hours, a level that reflects the sustained pressure placed on the team's capacity. One option that has been carefully considered is the replacement of half of that overtime, equivalent to 5% of paid hours, with one additional hire, at a fully loaded cost of $56k per year. It is important to note, however, that the overtime is not distributed evenly across the year; instead, it is heavily concentrated in two seasonal peaks, whereas a new hire would be paid for the full year, including the quieter periods when the additional capacity is simply not required. The $56k commitment is therefore a fixed one, while overtime spending flexes with demand from week to week. Overall, the choice involves a careful balancing of cost, flexibility, and cover at the peaks, and a fuller analysis of the peak workload pattern will be needed before a final view can be reached.
target: One additional hire, replacing half of the overtime in the quality laboratory, costs $56k per year fully loaded; the decision rests with laboratory management. The laboratory employs 18 full-time staff, and overtime was 10% of paid hours last year. Half of the overtime is 5% of paid hours. The trade-off is one of timing: the $56k is paid across the full year, while the overtime it displaces falls in two seasonal peaks. In the quieter months the hire adds capacity that the workload does not call for, and the post cannot be stood down when demand falls. Overtime, by contrast, is bought only in the weeks when the peaks arrive, and it can fall away altogether in a quiet year. The review sets a fixed annual salary cost against a variable overtime cost of the same stated size at the peaks, and the deciding evidence is the shape of the peak workload: how much of the peak overtime is concentrated enough, and predictable enough, to be covered by one person's contracted hours rather than bought week by week. The review draws on last year's paid-hours record for the overtime figure and on the fully loaded cost of the post for the hire figure; both are stated on the same annual basis so that the comparison is like for like. What the record does not show is absence cover or training time, and neither is priced in either figure.
